title: Schema Evolution Across an Event Bus
summary: Producers and consumers deploy independently, so a message schema has to change without breaking whoever hasn't upgraded yet.

slides.markdown:
An event bus has an unusual property: the producer publishing an event has no idea who all is consuming it, or when they'll next deploy. Unlike a single API where you control both ends of a call, changing an event's schema can silently break a consumer that hasn't upgraded yet — and you might not find out until it fails in production.

This topic is about the discipline that prevents that: distinguishing safe changes from breaking ones, and enforcing the rules automatically instead of trusting every producer to remember them.

slides.sectionTitle: Why schema change is harder on an event bus than behind a single API
slides.markdown:
Behind a single synchronous API, you can often coordinate both sides of a change — deploy the new server, deploy the new client, or run them side by side briefly during a rollout. You know exactly who calls you, because they're calling you right now. A dedicated API-versioning strategy exists for exactly that coordinated case.

On an event bus, the producer publishes into a topic that may have five consumer services, three of which haven't deployed in weeks and won't read the new schema until they do. There's no request/response to notice a mismatch in real time — a consumer might just silently misparse a renamed field and carry on with wrong data.

The practical implication: every schema change on an event bus has to assume some consumers are still running old code, possibly for a long time, and design for that instead of hoping for a coordinated deploy.

slides.sectionTitle: Backward-compatible vs forward-compatible schema changes: who breaks if you get it wrong
slides.markdown:
| | Backward-compatible change | Forward-compatible change |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | New consumers can read old messages | Old consumers can read new messages |
| Who breaks if violated | A new consumer trying to read an old message it doesn't understand | An old consumer trying to read a new message with fields it doesn't expect |
| Common example | Adding a field with a default (old messages just don't have it) | Adding an optional field (old consumers ignore fields they don't recognize) |
| Typical failure mode | New consumer crashes on a missing field with no default | Old consumer crashes trying to validate strictly against an old schema |

**How to decide:** you almost always need both directions at once, since old and new producers and consumers coexist during a rollout, so a safe schema evolution strategy has to preserve both, not just one.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an old consumer and a new consumer reading the same stream after a schema change
slides.markdown:
![An old consumer expecting schema v1 and a new consumer expecting schema v2 both read the same event stream, each tolerating fields it wasn't built for](assets/schema-v1-v2-consumers.svg)

Both consumers read from the same log; neither gets messages formatted just for it. The old consumer needs new messages to still look enough like v1 that it doesn't break; the new consumer needs to tolerate older messages that predate whatever v2 added.

This is why schema evolution is a two-way constraint, not a one-time migration — the stream has to remain readable by whichever version happens to be running, for however long that takes to fully roll out.

slides.sectionTitle: Schema registries: enforcing compatibility rules before a producer is allowed to publish
slides.markdown:
A **schema registry** (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry) sits in front of publishing: before a producer can push a message under a new schema version, the registry checks whether that new schema is compatible with the prior version, under a compatibility rule the topic owner configured — backward, forward, or full.

If a developer tries to publish a schema that removes a required field without a default, the registry rejects the publish outright — the incompatible change never reaches the topic, and no consumer ever sees the broken message.

This moves the safety check from "hope every engineer remembers the rules" to "the registry mechanically enforces them before anything ships," which is the only way this actually holds up across many teams and producers over time.

slides.sectionTitle: Safe changes vs breaking changes: adding an optional field vs renaming or removing one
slides.markdown:
**Safe**: adding a new optional field with a sensible default. Old consumers ignore a field they don't recognize; new consumers get a default when reading an old message that predates the field. **Safe**: adding a new event type entirely — nobody who wasn't already listening for it is affected.

**Breaking**: renaming a field. To an old consumer reading by field name, the renamed field simply looks *missing* — `customerId` disappearing because it became `userId` isn't backward compatible even though the data is technically still there under a new name.

**Breaking**: removing a required field, or changing a field's type, a string becoming a number. Both change what a consumer parsing the old shape will get, often silently — a numeric field parsed as a string might not error, it might just produce garbage.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a producer ships a "small" field rename that silently breaks every downstream consumer
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "It's just a field rename, `customerId` to `userId` — practically the same thing, low risk."

**Why it's wrong:** every consumer reading by field name sees `customerId` vanish. If none of them have a fallback, they either crash on a missing required field, or silently treat the customer as null or unknown and carry on with wrong data — and because it's an event bus, this can hit five different services on five different deploy schedules, discovered days apart as each one eventually processes the new shape.

**Correct model:** treat a rename as two changes, not one: add the new field alongside the old one, update consumers to read the new field, then remove the old field only once a schema registry (or manual audit) confirms every consumer has migrated.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: an Avro schema change that stays backward-compatible
The enum trap: adding a new value is a breaking change for old consumers
slides.markdown:
Enums feel like a safe, closed set of values, which is exactly why adding one is a common mistake. Say a `status` field is an enum of `PENDING`, `SHIPPED`, `CANCELLED`, and a producer adds `RETURNED`. Old consumer code that switches on all three original values, with no default branch, either throws on the unrecognized value or, worse, silently falls through a case statement and mishandles a returned order as if it were still pending.

This is subtle because it doesn't look like a schema change in the way a renamed field does — the *field* didn't change, only the set of legal values in it did. Some serialization formats (Avro) can enforce a default enum symbol for exactly this case; formats without that need every consumer to be written defensively, with an explicit "unknown value" branch, from the start.

The senior-level habit: treat every enum a producer controls as an open set from the consumer's side, and always code a fallback branch, even when the current schema looks exhaustive.
